question: What is the route of transmission?

options.A: The time it takes for a disease to show its first symptoms
options.B: The specific path a pathogen takes from its source to a new host
options.C: The total number of microbes required to cause an infection
options.D: The chemical makeup of an infectious agent's outer shell

explanation: The route of transmission is simply the way a germ travels from where it lives to a person who can catch it. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T81#GNS214_U1_T81_h1)

question: Why is knowing the route of transmission important for a nurse?

options.A: It eliminates the need for hand hygiene in clean wards
options.B: It predicts the exact day the patient will be discharged
options.C: It determines which antibiotic the doctor will prescribe first
options.D: It helps choose the correct isolation and barrier precautions

explanation: When nurses know how a germ travels, they can block that path using masks, gloves, or specific room placements. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T81#GNS214_U1_T81_h1)

question: Which of the following is the first link in the chain of infection?
explanation: The chain always starts with the actual germ or infectious agent itself before it finds a home. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T81#GNS214_U1_T81_h2)

question: What happens when a nurse washes their hands properly between patients?

options.A: It permanently cures the patient of chronic illnesses
options.B: It creates a new portal of entry for beneficial flora
options.C: It breaks the mode of transmission link in the chain
options.D: It destroys the genetic material of the reservoir host

explanation: Handwashing removes or kills germs, stopping them from traveling from one person to another. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T81#GNS214_U1_T81_h2)

question: What is a fomite in the context of infection control?

options.A: A specialized mask used for airborne disease isolation
options.B: A living insect that carries parasites to humans
options.C: An inanimate object that can transmit infectious agents
options.D: A chemical spray used to clean hospital floors

explanation: Fomites are non-living surfaces or objects like stethoscopes or tables that hold onto germs and pass them along. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T81#GNS214_U1_T81_h3)

question: A patient contracts a skin infection after touching a blood pressure cuff that was used on a previous infected patient without being cleaned. What type of transmission is this?
explanation: Because the germ traveled from the first patient to the cuff and then to the second patient, it is indirect contact through a fomite. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T81#GNS214_U1_T81_h3)

question: Why do airborne diseases require special negative-pressure rooms while droplet diseases do not?

options.A: Airborne particles stay suspended in the air and travel much farther
options.B: Droplet nuclei are too large to pass through standard hospital doors
options.C: Airborne pathogens only survive inside the human bloodstream
options.D: Droplet particles are heavy and require direct physical contact to spread

explanation: Tiny airborne nuclei float on air currents across rooms, whereas heavy droplets quickly drop to the ground within a short distance. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T81#GNS214_U1_T81_h4)

question: Which disease is classically transmitted via the airborne route?
explanation: Tuberculosis spreads through tiny airborne droplets released when an infected person coughs or speaks. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T81#GNS214_U1_T81_h4)

question: What is a biological vector?

options.A: A contaminated food supply that causes widespread food poisoning
options.B: An organism in which the pathogen multiplies or develops before infecting a human
options.C: A water pipe that carries treated municipal drinking water
options.D: A sterile surgical instrument used during sterile wound dressings

explanation: A biological vector is a living creature, like a mosquito, where the germ actually lives and grows part of its life cycle. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T81#GNS214_U1_T81_h5)

question: An entire village develops severe watery diarrhea after drinking from a well that was contaminated by floodwater. What type of transmission does this represent?
explanation: When many people get sick from a single shared source like water or food, it is classified as common vehicle transmission. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T81#GNS214_U1_T81_h5)

question: When should a nurse apply standard precautions in clinical practice?

options.A: Whenever a patient displays symptoms of an active fever
options.B: Exclusively in intensive care units and surgical theaters
options.C: Only when caring for patients with confirmed airborne diseases
options.D: For all patients receiving care, regardless of their diagnosis

explanation: Standard precautions are the baseline level of infection control used for every single patient interaction to prevent blood and fluid exposure. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T81#GNS214_U1_T81_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a standard precaution practice?

options.A: Using a private negative-pressure room for every patient
options.B: Performing hand hygiene before and after patient contact
options.C: Using safe injection practices and proper sharps disposal
options.D: Wearing gloves when touching non-intact skin or body fluids

explanation: Negative-pressure rooms are special transmission-based precautions for airborne germs, not a routine standard precaution for everyone. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T81#GNS214_U1_T81_h6)
